name: Retail Use Case
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: What Happened When Retailers Tried Blockchain Directly
lesson.summary: Beyond upstream supply chain tracing, retailers experimented with blockchain for shelf-level food traceability and consumer-facing NFT loyalty programs, and the food safety pilots have outlasted the NFT experiments by a wide margin.
lesson.body:
This chapter is closely related to the supply chain use case covered earlier, but it focuses specifically on the retailer-facing side: what happens in the store, in a customer's app, and in a brand's direct relationship with shoppers, rather than the upstream tracing between farms, processors, and distributors.

Carrefour, the large French retailer, ran one of the most well-documented retail blockchain programs, starting around 2018, using IBM Food Trust-style technology to let shoppers scan a QR code on products like chicken, eggs, and tomatoes and see the item's journey from farm to store shelf. Carrefour publicized measurable results tied to some of these tracked products, including reduced customer complaint rates, and the specific scope has evolved over time, so readers should treat exact current figures as something to verify independently rather than take at face value. This is one of the retail blockchain pilots that persisted rather than being quietly discontinued, and a reasonable explanation is that it served two purposes at once: genuine food-safety traceability, and a visible, marketable signal of transparency that shoppers could interact with directly in the store.

Retail's other major blockchain experiment, non-fungible token (NFT) based loyalty and brand engagement programs, has a much shorter track record. Starbucks Odyssey launched in December 2022 on the Polygon network, letting customers earn and purchase NFT "stamps" that unlocked rewards and branded experiences. Starbucks announced it was shutting the program down in March 2024. Nike pursued a related strategy after acquiring the virtual sneaker studio RTFKT in 2021 and launching its own .SWOOSH platform for NFT-backed virtual and physical products; Nike scaled back significant parts of this NFT strategy in the years that followed, though readers should treat the precise current status as something to check independently, since this is recent enough that public reporting continues to evolve. The pattern across these programs is consistent: they were launched as marketing and brand-engagement bets during the 2021 to 2022 period when NFTs were near the peak of their own hype cycle, not as attempts to solve any operational trust or verification problem, and most did not survive the cooling of NFT market enthusiasm that followed.

The contrast between these two retail stories is genuinely instructive. The programs that lasted, Carrefour-style food traceability being the clearest example, solved a real, unglamorous, operational problem involving actual multi-party trust (retailer, distributor, and farm each keeping their own separate records). The programs that did not last were riding a speculative asset trend rather than addressing a genuine business need, which connects directly back to the hype cycle chapter: retail NFT loyalty programs are about as clean an example as exists of a project launched right at the Peak of Inflated Expectations for a specific technology, in this case NFTs, rather than at a point where the underlying business case had already been proven out.
